# Draft:Second Italo-Senussi War

Draft in creation (test)
The Second Italo-Senussi War, It is also worth noting that, in some military sources, the conflict is called a "war of pacification." The Arabic designation is  /  (), or  /  (). The genocide committed by Fascist Italy in Cyrenaica is referred to by Libyans as  /  (), which is transliterated as "Shar" in English-language scholarly literature.|group=nb}} was Italy's decade-long campaign to conquer and colonize Tripolitania and Cyrenaica (modern Libya). Initially a liberal effort, then fascist from 1925/26, the war aimed to seize territory and establish Italian settlements by expropriating and expelling local Berber and Arab populations. The conflict escalated into genocide after 1929, particularly in Cyrenaica, where Italy employed area bombing, poison gas, mass executions, death marches, and the first fascist concentration camps.
Background
Italian colonialism and the First war of occupation
Italian colonialism in Africa began in 1882 in Eritrea but suffered a major defeat at Adwa in 1896, shifting focus to Libya (then Ottoman Tripolitania). Italy prepared for colonization through banks, schools, and trade from the 1890s onward. As part of its imperialist strategy, Italy resurrected the historical term "Libya" to justify colonial expansion, linking its claims to Rome's ancient dominion over the territory. In 1911, Italy demanded control of Tripolitania from the Ottoman Empire. When refused, the Italo-Turkish War began. Despite expecting easy victory, Italy faced fierce Ottoman-Tripolitanian resistance, and were forced to limit their controlled land to coastal areas. The 1912 Treaty of Ouchy ended the war ambiguously: Ottoman troops withdrew but sovereignty remained unclear until Turkey formally ceded Libya to Italy in the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne. Ahmed Sharif as-Senussi was the first guerrilla to organize the tribes to fight togheter for the jihad against the Italians in early 1913. Sulayman al-Baruni, initially choosing for a peaceful solution with the Italians, changed his mind and declared the self-enstablished Tripolitanian Republic, probably because of influence from local Arab guerrillas, who believed that the only solution for autonomy was a fight against the Italians. However, after his defeat at the battle of Al-Asaba'a on 23 March, the Republic had dissolved, and most of the Arab guerrillas that had fought in the battle fled to Fezzan to continue the resistance. This resistance too was eventually defeated at the battle of Mahrugah on 24 December.
The Italians successfully conquered northern Tripolitania and Fezzan mostly because of divisions among Arab and Berber populations and rivalries between Arab tribes that prevented unified resistance. In Cyrenaica, however, Italian forces remained confined to coastal areas, unable to penetrate territory where resistance coalesced around the Islamic Sufi Senussi Brotherhood led by Ahmed Sharif as-Senussi. The outbreak of World War I forced Italy to redeploy substantial troop contingents, significantly weakening occupation forces. In November 1914, rebellion erupted in Fezzan and quickly spread to northern Tripolitania. Combined forces from northern Tripolitania, Fezzan, and Cyrenaica defeated the Italian army in the battle of Gasr bu Hadi, driving it back to the coast. By summer 1915, Italian control had collapsed to just four port cities: Tripoli, Derna, Homs, and Benghazi. This humiliating contraction of Italy's colonial ambitions persisted beyond the end of World War I.
Formation of Arab republics in Libya

Weakened by its entry into World War I and pressured by Tripolitanian resistance, Italy was forced to make several concessions to Arabs and Berbers from 1915 onwards. Furthermore, two indigenous states formed during this period on the territory of formerly Ottoman Tripolitania: the Senussi Emirate in Cyrenaica and the Tripolitan Republic.
By late 1912, the Senussi leader Ahmed Sharif had relocated his headquarters from the southern oasis of Kufra to Jaghbub in the north, where he established an independent emirate founded on the Arab tribes of Cyrenaica. During World War I, Ottoman pressure compelled the militant pan-Islamic leader to launch attacks against British-controlled Egypt, a decision that severely damaged al-Sharif's standing with the British authorities. To enable a British-Senussi alliance against Italy, Ahmed Sharif stepped down as Senussi leader in 1916, replaced by his cousin Idris. Britain effectively recognized the Senussi as Cyrenaica's representatives. Through British-mediated negotiations, the 1917 Treaty of Acroma divided Cyrenaica between Italian coastal control and Senussi administration of the interior. However, this arrangement conflicted with the 1915 Treaty of London, in which Britain, France, and Russia had already promised Italy control over all of Tripolitania. Nevertheless, under the Treaty of Regima signed on 25 October 1920, Italy formally recognized Idris's hereditary title of Emir and acknowledged his territorial authority, with Ajdabiya serving as the administrative capital. In return, the Italians provided monthly stipends to Idris and his family, funded his general expenditures, and subsidized both his military and police forces.
In Tripolitania, the Italian withdrawal from the interior in 1914–1915 created a power vacuum that rival tribal leaders competed to fill. This precipitated widespread tribal conflict and territorial fragmentation. By 1916, two dominant factions had emerged: the Senussi Order, operating in the Sirte Desert, and Ramadan al-Shutaywi, who controlled northeastern Tripolitania. When the Senussi attempted to expand their influence across Tripolitania, they clashed with Asswehly, who decisively defeated them at the battle of Bani Walid. This defeat effectively confined Senussi influence outside Cyrenaica to portions of the Fezzan region. After the Ottomans finally withdrew from Tripolitania in 1918, the tribes found themselves without strong external allies, unlike the Senussi Order in Cyrenaica, which enjoyed British support. Consequently, the tribal leaders forged a consensus on establishing a pan-Tripolitan government and proclaimed the Tripolitan Republic in Msallata in November 1918, with Misrata as its capital—marking the first formally democratic government in an Arab country. Built on a pan-Islamic ideology, the republic was governed collectively by four prominent tribal leaders through the "Council of the Republic," a compromise necessitated by the tribes' inability to agree on a single leader. The Egyptian pan-Arab nationalist Abdul Rahman Azzam served as an advisor to the government. With the Tripolitan Republic, Libya saw the establishment of its second indigenous state, following the Senussi Emirate in Cyrenaica.

As early as 1917, Italy granted the Tripolitanians limited self-governing rights. In 1919, they successfully negotiated a peace treaty with the colonial authorities that provided Tripolitania with a parliament, press freedom, and citizenship for the Muslim population. In spring 1920, the Tripolitanian government launched a military campaign to consolidate its authority over all Tripolitan tribes, precipitating another civil war. This conflict was resolved only in November 1920 through the Gharyan Agreement, which replaced the original Council of the Republic with a Reform Committee as the new governing body. The agreement explicitly rejected any Italian claims to sovereignty over Tripolitania. Beyond the Italian-controlled coastal cities, and even within certain areas of Tripolitania itself, the Reform Committee issued decrees and collected taxes and other levies. However, since Italy had already secured its colonial claims to Tripolitania through treaties with Great Britain and France, no other state recognized the fledgling republic. Unable to mount effective resistance against the Italians, Tripolitania's leaders offered sovereignty over their territory to the Senussi leader Idris, who had by then been recognized by Italy as Emir of Cyrenaica, in December 1921.
War
The 1922 campaign
In response to Tripolitania's attempt to forge an anti-Italian alliance with Cyrenaica under Senussi leadership, Governor Giuseppe Volpi launched a reconquest campaign on 26 January 1922. An Italian force of 1,500 men landed near Misrata, capturing the port and its 200 defenders after seventeen days of fighting. Within a week, the Tripolitanian Reform Committee declared jihad and called for attacks on all Italian positions. The railway to Tripoli was severed, an Italian Eritrean Askari unit in ʽAziziya came under siege, and numerous smaller clashes erupted across the territory. Following a government crisis in Rome and the appointment of Giovanni Amendola as Colonial Minister, a ceasefire was brokered in late February while Rome deliberated its next strategy. Egypt's declaration of independence from Great Britain in March 1922 galvanized the Tripolitanians. Recognizing their dependence on Senussi support, Tripolitan envoys attended a gathering of Cyrenaican tribal leaders in Ajdabiya, where they offered King Idris sovereignty over Tripolitania. On 22 June, the Tripolitan delegation officially proclaimed Idris as Emir, though he did not formally accept the title until 22 September.
After the armistice ended on 10 April 1922, Governor Volpi, now enjoying full backing from Rome, prepared for the next operations. His force of 15,000 soldiers confronted approximately 7,000 resistance fighters who launched an assault at Zawiya. Colonel Rodolfo Graziani, one of several capable officers Volpi had assembled, successfully secured the coastal strip from Tripoli to Zuwara within ten days. Graziani revolutionized desert warfare through rapid mechanized advances supported by air power and marked by ruthless brutality. Under the command of General Pietro Badoglio, a decorated World War I veteran newly arrived in Tripoli, Graziani relieved the besieged city of ʽAziziya on 30 April. By mid-May, Italian forces had secured the Jafara plain, killing 6,000 Tripolitanian fighting men in the process. In late May, Graziani launched the so-called "pacification" of the western Jebal Nafusa mountains, capturing Nalut on 5 June. Governor Volpi, having abandoned negotiations with Tripolitan representatives, imposed martial law across Tripolitania, effectively a formal declaration of war. Mussolini's March on Rome in October 1922 initially had little impact on the campaign. On 31 October, Graziani reported taking Yafran, followed in November by the conquest of the entire mountainous region stretching from Nalut to Gharyan.
Mussolini's Colonial Policy and the 1923–1924 campaign
Fascist Italy transformed its inherited colonial tradition into aggressive settler colonialism characterized by centralized control, mass Italian resettlement, racist ideology, and unprecedented violence against indigenous populations. Historians debate when Mussolini's fascist phase of colonization began; whether immediately after his 1922 accession, with the 1923 termination of Senussi autonomy treaties, or on 15 April 1926, when Mussolini delivered a major programmatic speech in Tripoli celebrating Italian conquests and outlining colonial ambitions.
Beyond subjugating rebellious tribes, Mussolini's imperial policy sought to provide Italy with "living space" and fulfill its "historical mission" by establishing settlement colonies modeled on ancient Rome. His grand vision encompassed controlling northern Africa from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic and the Horn of Africa. However, Italy's military and economic weakness initially forced consolidation of existing territories. Under the slogan La Riconquista Fascista della Libia (), the government launched a massive military campaign aimed at complete "pacification" and widespread population expulsion to enable Italian colonization.
The general offensive launched on 29 January 1923, achieved rapid success: Tarhuna fell by 5 February, followed by an advance through Zliten to Misrata, captured on February 26. Italian air forces bombed Arab refugee columns exceeding 2,000 people fleeing Zliten. However, operations extending into eastern and southern Tripolitania initially faced difficulties, but internal divisions among Tripolitanian leaders weakened resistance. While Ahmad Sayf al-Nasr collaborated with the Senussi, other insurgent leaders like Abd al-Nabi Bilkhayr and Ramadan al-Shutaywi opposed Senussi presence in Tripolitania. From spring 1923, the reconquest grew increasingly brutal. Many tribes fled into the Sirte Desert, while leaders sought refuge in Tunisia and Egypt. Bani Walid fell in December 1923, Ghadames in February 1924, and the capture of Mizda in May 1924 completed the "pacification" of northern Tripolitania. Rodolfo Graziani was promoted to general as the campaign's celebrated "hero." The southern Fezzan region, instead, became a refuge for most resisting Tripolitanian tribes. Allied with the Fezzanian Awlad Sulayman tribe, they waged an effective guerrilla war, avoiding open battle in favor of small-unit tactics. Operating primarily at night, they conducted sabotage operations, ambushed convoys, and raided military stations through brief skirmishes that exploited their mobility and knowledge of the terrain.
